replacement: “The court has resolved to go on with the trial. Meanwhile, I would like to make a few remarks on the portrait of Smerdyakov that the prosecutor drew with such subtlety and talent. I admire his talent, but I cannot agree with him. I have visited Smerdyakov. I have seen him and talked with him, and he made quite a different impression on me. His health was weak, it is true. But in character, in spirit, he was far from the weak man the prosecutor has made of him. I found no sign of the timidity the prosecutor made so much of. Nor was he simple. On the contrary, I found an extreme distrust, hidden behind a mask of _naïveté_, and a mind of considerable reach. The prosecutor was too simple in taking him for feeble-minded. He made a very definite impression on me, and I came away convinced that he was a plainly spiteful creature, wildly ambitious, vengeful, and intensely envious. I made some inquiries. He resented his birth and was ashamed of it, and he would grind his teeth when he remembered that he was the son of ‘stinking Lizaveta.’ He was disrespectful to the servant Grigory and his wife, who had looked after him in his childhood. He cursed Russia and sneered at it. He dreamed of going to France and becoming a Frenchman. He often used to say that he had not the money for it. I believe he loved no one but himself, and he held a strangely high opinion of himself. His whole notion of culture came down to good clothes, clean shirt-fronts and polished boots. He believed himself to be Fyodor Pavlovitch’s illegitimate son (there is evidence of this), and he might well have resented his position beside his master’s legitimate sons. They had everything, and he had nothing. They had every right, they had the inheritance, while he was only the cook. He told me himself that he had helped Fyodor Pavlovitch put the notes into the envelope. The purpose of that sum—a sum that would have made his career—must have been hateful to him. Besides, he saw three thousand roubles in new rainbow-colored notes. (I asked him about that on purpose.) Oh, beware of showing an ambitious and envious man a great sum of money all at once! And it was the first time he had seen so much money in one man’s hands. The sight of those rainbow-colored notes may have left a morbid mark on his imagination, but with no immediate result.

“The prosecutor asks at what moment Smerdyakov could have committed the murder. But it is very easy to name that moment. He might have woken out of a deep sleep (for he was only asleep—an epileptic fit is always followed by deep sleep) at the very moment when old Grigory shouted at the top of his voice, ‘Parricide!’ That shout in the dark and the silence may have woken Smerdyakov, whose sleep may by then have been lighter. He might quite naturally have woken up an hour earlier.

“But do you want to punish him fearfully, terribly, with the most awful punishment imaginable, and at the same time to save him and give his soul new birth? If so, overwhelm him with your mercy! You will see, you will hear, how he trembles and is struck with horror. ‘How can I bear this mercy? How can I bear so much love? Am I worthy of it?’ That is what he will cry out.
